justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to recent observed prices, expecting minimal deviation given typical intraday mean-reversion and the absence of any imminent scheduled catalysts. The one-week estimate nudged slightly higher, incorporating a mild positive drift assumption consistent with recent momentum while acknowledging that short-term consolidation was equally plausible. The one-month estimate extended that drift further, reflecting a baseline assumption that the underlying trend remained constructive, though with diminishing conviction as the horizon extended and more macro variables came into play.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the interval is relatively tight because price behavior over a single session tends to be constrained by liquidity and the absence of major scheduled news. By one week, the interval widens to account for the possibility of earnings releases, macroeconomic data prints, or shifts in sector sentiment that could materially reprice the asset. By one month, the interval nearly doubles in half-width compared to the daily case, reflecting the accumulation of unknown unknowns — geopolitical developments, Federal Reserve commentary, broader equity market rotations, and idiosyncratic company-level events that are difficult to anticipate from a snapshot in time.

There are several tail risks that could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals in either direction. On the downside, a sharp deterioration in risk appetite — triggered by a surprise inflation print, a credit event, or an escalation in geopolitical tensions — could drive prices significantly below the lower bound of even the monthly interval. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings report, a positive analyst catalyst, or a broad market rally fueled by dovish central bank signals could push prices above the upper bound. My intervals were deliberately set at the 90% confidence level, meaning I explicitly acknowledged a 10% probability of outcomes outside those bounds, and in practice, fat-tailed financial distributions make those extreme scenarios somewhat more likely than a normal distribution would suggest.
